li-short.title: Lithium-ion battery

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A lithium-ion battery stores energy through reversible chemical changes.
Lithium ions move between two electrodes when the battery charges and discharges.

sections.title: Construction
bullets: Negative electrode: graphite containing lithium stored between graphite layers (LiₓC₆ when charged). Positive electrode: a lithium metal oxide; LiCoO₂ is the example used here.
A separator with tiny pores prevents direct electrical contact while allowing Li⁺ transport. A lithium-salt organic electrolyte conducts ions; copper and aluminium foils collect current.

sections.title: Discharging: the cell supplies current
bullets: At the negative electrode (anode): LiₓC₆ → C₆ + xLi⁺ + xe⁻.
At the positive electrode (cathode): Li₁₋ₓCoO₂ + xLi⁺ + xe⁻ → LiCoO₂.
Overall: LiₓC₆ + Li₁₋ₓCoO₂ → C₆ + LiCoO₂. Li⁺ travels through the electrolyte; electrons travel through the external load.

sections.title: Applications
bullets: Mobile phones, laptops and other rechargeable portable devices.
Rechargeable energy-storage packs; electric vehicles use suitable Li-ion chemistries such as LFP or NMC rather than necessarily this LiCoO₂ example.

bomb.title: Bomb calorimeter: construction, working and GCV

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A bomb calorimeter finds the heat released when a known mass of fuel burns completely.
We calculate this heat from the rise in water temperature.

sections.title: Principle and construction
bullets: A known mass of fuel burns completely in excess oxygen inside a sealed, rigid steel bomb.
Heat released is absorbed by a measured mass of water and the calorimeter.
The condensed product water makes this a gross calorific value measurement.
Parts: steel bomb, oxygen inlet, crucible, ignition wire/electrodes, water bucket, stirrer, thermometer and insulating jacket.

sections.title: Working
bullets: Weigh fuel of mass m into the crucible and arrange the ignition wire.
Seal the oxygen-filled bomb and immerse it in water of mass W. Record initial temperature t₁.
Ignite electrically, stir the water, and record maximum temperature t₂. Determine cooling and auxiliary-heat corrections.

sections.title: Heat balance and derived expression
bullets: Let w be the water equivalent of the calorimeter; c the cooling correction in °C; eₐ, e𝒻 and eₜ the acid, fuse-wire and thread heat corrections in calories.
With W, w and m in grams, water heat capacity is 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
m × GCV + eₐ + e𝒻 + eₜ = (W+w)[(t₂−t₁)+c].
So GCV = {(W+w)[(t₂−t₁)+c] − (eₐ+e𝒻+eₜ)} / m, in cal/g.
Cooling correction is added to temperature rise; heat from acid formation, wire and thread is subtracted because it is not the desired fuel contribution.
For SI calculations, use consistent masses, heat capacities and joules.

sections.title: Relation to NCV
bullets: NCV = GCV − 0.09H × L, where H is mass percent hydrogen and L is latent heat per gram of water when GCV is in cal/g. Moisture corrections are added separately if supplied.

m × GCV + eₐ + e𝒻 + eₜ = (W+w)[(t₂−t₁)+c].
So GCV = {(W+w)[(t₂−t₁)+c] − (eₐ+e𝒻+eₜ)} / m, in cal/g.
Cooling correction is added to temperature rise; heat from acid formation, wire and thread is subtracted because it is not the desired fuel contribution.
For SI calculations, use consistent masses, heat capacities and joules.


Relation to NCV
NCV = GCV − 0.09H × L, where H is mass percent hydrogen and L is latent heat per gram of water when GCV is in cal/g. Moisture corrections are added separately if supplied.

nernst.title: Derive the Nernst equation

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: The Nernst equation tells us how the cell voltage changes when conditions differ from standard conditions.
Start with the free-energy relation and rearrange it step by step.

sections.title: Thermodynamic starting point
bullets: For a balanced cell reaction, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. The electrical work relations are ΔG = −nFE and ΔG° = −nFE°.
Here n is the number of electrons in the balanced reaction, F the Faraday constant, R the gas constant, T the absolute temperature and Q the reaction quotient in activities.

sections.title: Substitute and rearrange
bullets: −nFE = −nFE° + RT ln Q.
Divide by −nF: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q.
Using ln Q = 2.303 log₁₀Q: E = E° − (2.303RT/nF) log₁₀Q.

sections.title: At 298 K
bullets: With R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and F ≈ 96485 C mol⁻¹: E = E° − (0.05916/n) log₁₀Q volts.

sections.title: Single metal electrode
bullets: For Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M(s), Q = 1/a(Mⁿ⁺), because the activity of a pure solid is 1.
E = E° + (0.05916/n) log₁₀a(Mⁿ⁺) at 298 K. In a dilute ideal solution, activity is approximated by concentration relative to the standard concentration.

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: To calculate cell voltage, use a balanced reaction and a consistent sign convention for electrode potentials.
The printed question has errors, so the stated and corrected interpretations are shown separately.

bullets: The paper prints Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → Fe + Cl₂, with E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) = −0.440 V. The equation is not charge-balanced, and −0.440 V is normally associated with Fe²⁺/Fe, not Fe³⁺/Fe.

gcv-ncv.title: Gross and net calorific values

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: GCV includes heat recovered when water vapour condenses. NCV excludes that heat.
Therefore GCV is greater than NCV when the fuel produces water.

sections.title: GCV / higher calorific value
bullets: Heat released by complete combustion of unit mass of fuel when products return to the reference temperature and the water formed is condensed.
The recovered heat includes water-vapour condensation.

sections.title: NCV / lower calorific value
bullets: Heat released when product water remains vapour.
The latent heat of that water is not recovered.

sections.title: Why GCV exceeds NCV
bullets: For a fuel producing water, GCV − NCV equals the unrecovered latent heat.
1 g hydrogen produces 9 g water. If H is mass percent hydrogen, water formed per gram fuel = 9H/100 = 0.09H g. So NCV = GCV − 0.09H × L, using compatible units.
For a dry fuel producing no water, the values coincide; “GCV is always strictly greater” needs water formation or moisture.

gas-solar.title: Gaseous fuels and solar cells

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Gaseous fuels mix readily with air and their flow is easy to control. A solar cell converts light directly into electricity.

sections.title: A. Advantages of gaseous fuels
bullets: Mix readily with air, allowing controlled, more complete combustion and less excess air.
Produce no ash or clinker when clean gas is used, reducing furnace cleaning.
Gas flow is easily metered; flame and temperature can be adjusted quickly.
Pipelines and automatic burners simplify handling; no coal crushing or liquid atomization is needed.
Limitations: low volumetric energy density, leakage risk and storage requirements. Gases are not universally superior on every measure.

sections.title: B. Solar cell: principle and construction
bullets: A solar cell converts light directly into DC electricity by the photovoltaic effect. A silicon p–n junction, metal contacts and a light-facing surface form a basic cell.

sections.title: C. Working and applications
bullets: Absorbed photons create electron–hole pairs.
The junction electric field separates charge; contacts collect it and current flows through an external load.
Cells form modules and arrays for rooftop systems, lighting, remote equipment and satellites.
Output varies with illumination, so night-time use needs storage or another supply.

bullets: Flame photometry identifies or measures certain metal ions using the light they emit in a flame.

sections.title: Definition and principle
bullets: Flame photometry is atomic emission analysis: a flame excites atoms of an element, and their characteristic emitted light is measured.
Over a calibrated working range, emission intensity relates to concentration.

sections.title: Instrument and working
bullets: Nebulizer converts the sample solution to a fine spray. The burner/flame evaporates solvent, atomizes the salt and excites some atoms.

A photodetector converts light into an electrical signal. Measure a blank and standards, then determine the unknown from the calibration curve.

sections.title: Applications
bullets: Determination of sodium, potassium and lithium in suitable solutions.
Analysis of water, soil extracts and fertilizer samples.
Clinical electrolyte analysis where the instrument and method are validated.

sections.title: Limitation
bullets: Matrix effects, interfering emission and self-absorption can affect results.
Use appropriate dilution, calibration and sample preparation.

sofc.title: Solid oxide fuel cell

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A solid oxide fuel cell uses a solid ceramic electrolyte at high temperature.
Chemical reactions produce electricity as ions cross the electrolyte and electrons flow through the external circuit.

sections.title: Construction
bullets: A dense ceramic electrolyte such as yttria-stabilized zirconia conducts O²⁻ ions between a porous fuel electrode (often Ni–ceramic) and a porous oxygen electrode.
It operates at elevated temperature.

sections.title: Hydrogen-fuel working
bullets: Cathode: O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻. Oxide ions cross the solid electrolyte toward the fuel electrode.
Anode: 2H₂ + 2O²⁻ → 2H₂O + 4e⁻. Electrons travel through the external load back to the cathode.
Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O + electrical energy + heat.

sections.title: Features and applications
bullets: High-temperature exhaust can supply useful heat in combined heat and power systems.
Solid electrolyte avoids liquid-electrolyte leakage; suitable systems can use reformed fuels.
Used for stationary/distributed generation and auxiliary power.
High temperature imposes materials and thermal-cycling constraints; startup is slower than in low-temperature fuel cells.

bullets: Hydrogen and oxygen undergo electrochemical reaction at separate porous catalytic electrodes.

sections.title: Conduction in polyacetylene

pla.title: Biodegradable polymers and PLA

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Biodegradable polymers can break down through biological action under suitable conditions. PLA, or polylactic acid, is one example; it often needs controlled composting conditions to break down efficiently.

sections.title: Definition
bullets: Biodegradable polymers can be broken down through biological activity, often following hydrolysis, into smaller molecules that can undergo further metabolism.
Examples include PLA, PGA and PHB.
Biodegradability depends on conditions.

sections.title: PLA synthesis
bullets: Polylactic acid (PLA) is an aliphatic polyester derived from lactic acid, HO–CH(CH₃)–COOH.
Direct condensation forms ester links and removes water: n HO–CH(CH₃)–COOH → HO–CH(CH₃)–CO–[O–CH(CH₃)–CO]ₙ₋₁–OH + (n−1)H₂O.
High-molecular-weight PLA is also made by ring-opening polymerization of lactide, the cyclic dimer.
The repeat unit is [–O–CH(CH₃)–CO–]ₙ.

sections.title: Properties
bullets: Thermoplastic polyester; often transparent, relatively stiff and brittle.
Ester bonds can hydrolyse; rate depends on temperature, water, molecular weight and crystallinity.
Many grades soften near 50–60 °C; thermal behaviour varies with stereochemistry and grade.
Biocompatible grades are used in selected medical products. Compostability does not mean rapid degradation in ordinary soil or seawater.

sections.title: Applications
bullets: Packaging films, containers and disposable articles where suitable recovery/composting systems exist.
3D-printing filament.
Resorbable sutures, fixation devices and drug-delivery systems with appropriate medical-grade material.

green12.title: Twelve principles of green chemistry

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Green chemistry aims to reduce waste and hazards when chemicals are made and used.
The twelve principles guide better choices from raw materials to final products.

sections.title: Green chemistry
bullets: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste.

sections.title: Twelve principles
bullets: Prevention: avoid producing waste rather than cleaning it up later.
Atom economy: retain as many reactant atoms as possible in the desired product.
Less hazardous synthesis: choose routes with lower toxicity.
Safer chemicals: preserve function while reducing hazards.
Safer solvents and auxiliaries: avoid unnecessary solvents; choose less hazardous ones.
Energy efficiency: reduce energy demand and use mild conditions when feasible.
Renewable feedstocks: prefer renewable raw materials where practicable.
Reduce derivatives: avoid unnecessary protection/deprotection steps.
Catalysis: prefer selective catalytic routes over stoichiometric reagents.
Design for degradation: products should break down to less harmful substances after use.
Real-time analysis: monitor processes to prevent hazardous by-products.
Inherently safer processes: choose substances and conditions that reduce fire, explosion and release risks.

sections.title: Atom economy explained
bullets: Atom economy = stoichiometric mass of desired product / total stoichiometric mass of reactants × 100. It is a theoretical measure, not percentage yield.
Example: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ has 100% atom economy when ethane is the desired product, because all reactant atoms enter it.

sections.title: Catalysis explained
bullets: A catalyst accelerates a reaction without being consumed in the net reaction. A selective catalyst can reduce unwanted by-products and allow lower temperature.
Example: catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene with H₂ avoids stoichiometric reducing-agent waste.
Actual environmental benefit still depends on catalyst, solvent, energy and recovery.

maos-short.title: Microwave-assisted organic synthesis

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Microwave-assisted organic synthesis uses microwave energy to heat a reaction mixture.
Suitable materials absorb that energy and become hot.

sections.title: Meaning and heating mechanism
bullets: MAOS uses microwave energy to heat a reaction mixture through dipolar polarization and ionic conduction.
Microwave absorption depends on the mixture; it is not simply heating every substance equally.

sections.title: Merits and limitations
bullets: Rapid heating can shorten reaction time and improve throughput.
Selected reactions use less solvent or give fewer by-products; this must be demonstrated for the particular process.
Weakly absorbing mixtures heat poorly; scaling and penetration can be difficult.
Pressure and temperature need control in suitable laboratory reactors; microwave use is not automatically greener.

sections.title: Examples
bullets: Microwave-assisted esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, with appropriate catalyst and conditions.
Microwave-assisted condensation: an aldehyde and an active-methylene compound form an alkene product (Knoevenagel reaction), often with a suitable catalyst.
These are reaction classes, not universal recipes.

ultrasound.title: Ultrasound-assisted organic reactions

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Ultrasound can help reactions by forming tiny bubbles that grow and collapse in a liquid.
Their collapse creates strong local effects and improves mixing.

sections.title: Definition
bullets: Ultrasound-assisted synthesis applies sound above the audible range to a reaction medium.
In liquids, acoustic cavitation—bubble formation, growth and collapse—can improve mixing and generate intense local conditions.

sections.title: How it helps
bullets: Bubble collapse produces local heating and pressure and can accelerate mass transfer.
Microjets and agitation improve contact between immiscible liquids or between liquids and solid surfaces.
Reaction times can decrease, but improvements depend on frequency, power, solvent, vessel and chemistry.

sections.title: Example: esterification
bullets: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O, with an acid catalyst.
Published work demonstrates ultrasound-assisted esterification of aliphatic carboxylic acids with methanol or ethanol.
Cavitation improves contact and can accelerate the catalysed transformation.
Ultrasound supplies energy; it is not a reactant.

sections.title: Benefits and limitations
bullets: Potential benefits include faster conversion and milder bulk conditions.
Scale-up and energy efficiency need evaluation; ultrasound does not guarantee a greener process.

cnt.title: Carbon nanotubes: types, synthesis and properties

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A carbon nanotube is a tiny hollow tube made of carbon.
It can have one wall or several walls, and its structure controls its properties.

sections.title: Definition and types
bullets: A carbon nanotube (CNT) is a hollow cylindrical carbon nanostructure whose wall resembles a rolled graphene sheet.
SWCNT: a single cylindrical wall. MWCNT: several nested cylindrical walls separated by roughly the graphite interlayer distance.

sections.title: CVD synthesis
bullets: Feed a carbon-containing gas into a heated chamber containing catalyst nanoparticles such as Fe, Co or Ni.
Starting material decomposition provides carbon that starts to form and grows into tubes at the catalyst.
Control temperature, catalyst and gas flow to influence diameter and growth; remove unwanted carbon/catalyst as needed.

sections.title: Properties
bullets: High axial strength and stiffness at low density; actual composite strength depends on defects and dispersion.
Electrical behaviour depends on structure and the way the carbon sheet is wrapped, especially for SWCNTs; some are metallic and others semiconducting.
High axial thermal conductivity and large length-to-width ratio.
High surface area and useful field-emission/electrochemical behaviour.

sections.title: Applications
bullets: Conductive and reinforcing composites, sensors, electrodes and research electronic devices.
Performance depends on purity, alignment and processing.

fullerene.text:
Fullerenes: structure, properties and applications
Understand the idea
A fullerene is a closed cage of carbon atoms. C60 has a football-like shape made of pentagons and hexagons.


Structure
Fullerenes are closed-cage carbon molecules.
Buckminsterfullerene C₆₀ has 60 carbon atoms arranged as 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, like a football.
Each carbon has three carbon neighbours.


Properties
Hollow molecular cage with a system of linked bonds with electrons that can spread along it; can accept electrons.
C₆₀ is poorly soluble in water but dissolves in some organic solvents.
Chemical adding chemical groups changes solubility and electronic properties.
Pristine and doped fullerene solids differ electrically; certain alkali-doped compounds show superconductivity at low temperature.


Applications and research
Electron-accepting materials and derivatives in organic electronic/photovoltaic research.
Functionalized cages for molecular encapsulation and sensing studies.
Lubrication and specialized material additives are studied.
Drug-delivery and biomedical uses in the notes are research directions, not evidence that untreated fullerenes are approved medicines or universally nontoxic.

ev.title: EV battery: explanatory note

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: An electric vehicle battery pack supplies energy to the motor.
Many cells are connected together to provide the required voltage and capacity.

sections.title: Electric-vehicle battery
bullets: An EV traction battery stores electrical energy for the motor.
It is a pack of cells arranged in series for voltage and in parallel for capacity/current.
Li-ion is a common chemistry family; LFP and nickel-containing chemistries have different tradeoffs.

sections.title: Main requirements
bullets: High usable energy for range and enough power for acceleration.
Long cycle life and reliable performance across temperatures.
Battery-management electronics monitor cell voltage, temperature and charge balance.
Thermal control and protection against overcharge, deep discharge and excessive current.

sections.title: Charging and discharge
bullets: Charging stores energy through reversible electrode reactions; discharge supplies DC power to the vehicle electronics.
Regenerative braking can return some kinetic energy to the battery.
